overview: Fences is a 22-line wire-silent module that re-arms the vanilla sneak edge-clamp without sneaking. The Rise 6.1.30 fork patches Entity.moveEntity (lines 692-742) to fire a SafeWalkEvent with a default probe height of -1.0 before the clamp loop, and Fences listens on that event to set mc.thePlayer.safeWalk true and raise the probe height to -5. Vanilla only edge-clamps when the player is on the ground, sneaking, and would step off a ledge with no block within 1 block below; Fences applies the same clamp to a walking player and probes 5 blocks down, so the player stops at any ledge unless the drop is deeper than 5 blocks. The clamp zeroes the x/z motion component locally, the positions carried by the normal C03 stream simply stop at the edge, and no packet is emitted or modified.

sections.p: Entity.moveEntity computes the raw x/z displacement, then fires SafeWalkEvent(-1.0) and reads the event's height. The clamp that follows zeroes x, then z, then both together in 0.05 steps while the box offset by (x, height, z) finds no collision: the vanilla condition is onGround plus isSneaking on an EntityPlayer, and Fences contributes the safeWalk flag that extends the same loop to a non-sneaking player. safeWalk is reset to false at the end of every moveEntity call (line 742), which is exactly why the module needs a per-event listener: it re-arms the flag on every single move. The probe height of -5 means the loop only lets the player pass the edge when a block exists within 5 blocks below the feet, turning the module into invisible fences at cliffs up to 5 blocks deep.

The module emits nothing. The clamp edits the local motion before the position update is sent, so the C03 stream shows the player's positions stopping at the block edge: the same stream a player who simply released the movement key produces. The one structural difference from legitimate play is that vanilla edge-clamping is tied to the sneak state and therefore normally accompanies C0B sneak toggles, while Fences delivers the clamp with zero C0B traffic. No packet is cancelled, injected or rewritten, and the onGround flags that travel with the movement are genuine because the player remains on the ledge.

Server-side, an edge-clamped player is indistinguishable from a cautious one: the server never observes the would-be fall, because the position packets never leave the edge. There is no expected-fall state for an anticheat to key on, and the sent positions are always physically valid, so no movement envelope can fire. The module is a first-class example of a cheat with no wire presence; the countering set below documents the closest checks and why each one stays silent.

files.label: Fences.java
files.explanation: The entire module. A SafeWalkEvent listener sets mc.thePlayer.safeWalk to true and the event height to -5, and onDisable resets the flag. The event is fired from the fork's Entity.moveEntity (line 692) with a default height of -1.0 right before the sneak edge-clamp loop, and the module's height value widens the probe so the clamp holds at ledges up to 5 blocks deep. The module has no packet code at all; the effect is the local position clamping that the C03 stream then carries.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement physics envelope)
countering.explanation: SurvivalFly rebuilds the physics envelope from the world: horizontal allowance from prepareSpeedEstimation, vertical from vDistRel, violation (max(hDistanceAboveLimit, 0) plus max(yDistanceAboveLimit, 0)) times 100, and ground state from the block cache at minY minus yOnGround rather than from the packet flag. The Fences clamp produces exactly the movement the envelope expects: positions that stop on solid ground, onGround flags that match the ray-traced ground, and vertical deltas of zero while on the ledge. The instant stop at the edge is the same profile as a wall collision or a released key, both of which the model tolerates because it only bounds acceleration upward. The check is a boundary: it would fire the moment the clamp failed and the player fell, which is the one outcome the module prevents.

countering.label: Speed (prev-speed progression)
countering.explanation: Hawk Speed is a one-directional gain bound: expected equals friction times lastSpeed plus maxForce plus epsilon, and only moves that exceed the expected progression accumulate discrepancy toward the 0.1 threshold. The edge-clamp's instant deceleration is invisible to it by construction, because the check never punishes a speed drop: players stop at walls and release keys all the time, and both produce the same friction-decayed profile the model treats as legitimate. A player walking along a cliff with Fences active sends a steady at-speed stream until the edge, then a zero-delta move, which is precisely the deceleration the model allows. The check only becomes relevant if the module ever produced an acceleration the physics model cannot derive from input force, which the input-level clamp never does.

countering.label: Speed (horizontal accumulator)
countering.explanation: Arc v2's Speed check scores each move against the walking expectation built from baseMove 0.2873, speed potions, stage allowances and pending velocity, with an instant cancel above 8 blocks per move. The Fences clamp keeps every move inside that envelope: at-walk speed along the ledge, then an instant stop, and the stop is indistinguishable from a released key because the check has no input state to compare against. The on-ground accumulator sees a grounded player whose horizontal distance per tick never exceeds the expected walk speed, so no violation accumulates. Like the other movement checks in this set, it is an honest boundary: it can only fire on motion the clamp does not produce.

countering.label: GroundSpoof (claimed vs predicted ground)
countering.explanation: Grim's GroundSpoof flags when the claimed onGround flag contradicts the post-prediction ground state, with exemptions for spectator mode, exemptOnGround, block offsets and the teleport tick. The Fences clamp keeps the player genuinely grounded: every claim rides on the player standing on the ledge, so the predicted ground (derived from the last accepted position and the world collision) agrees with the claimed flag on every tick. The one hypothetical mismatch, claiming grounded while actually over the drop, is exactly what the clamp prevents from happening in the first place. The check stays silent, and the honest summary is that no server-side check can observe the module at all.
